arXiv:0809.3985v1 [cond-mat.dis-nn] 23 Sep 2008

Critical interfaces in the random-bond Potts model

Jesper L. Jacobsen Affiliation: CNRS-Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de l’Ecole Normale Supérieure, 24 rue Lhomond, 75231 Paris, France.    Pierre Le Doussal Affiliation: CNRS-Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de l’Ecole Normale Supérieure, 24 rue Lhomond, 75231 Paris, France.    Marco Picco Affiliation: CNRS-LPTHE, Universités Paris 6 et Paris 7, 4 Place Jussieu, 75005 Paris, France    Raoul Santachiara Affiliation: CNRS-Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de l’Ecole Normale Supérieure, 24 rue Lhomond, 75231 Paris, France.    Kay Jörg Wiese Affiliation: CNRS-Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de l’Ecole Normale Supérieure, 24 rue Lhomond, 75231 Paris, France.
Abstract

We study geometrical properties of interfaces in the random-temperature qq-states Potts model as an example of a conformal field theory weakly perturbed by quenched disorder. Using conformal perturbation theory in q−2q-2 we compute the fractal dimension of Fortuin Kasteleyn domain walls. We also compute it numerically both via the Wolff cluster algorithm for q=3q=3 and via transfer-matrix evaluations. We also obtain numerical results for the fractal dimension of spin clusters interfaces for q=3q=3. These are found numerically consistent with the duality κspin​κFK=16\kappa^{\mathrm{spin}}\kappa^{\mathrm{FK}}=16 as expressed in putative SLE parameters.

The discovery of the Schramm Löwner Evolution (SLE) has strongly revived interest in geometrical properties of interfaces in 2-dimensional statistical physics. SLE provides a rigorous classification, with a single parameter κ\kappa, of probability measures on non-crossing random fractal curves, which satisfy both conformal invariance and the domain Markov property [1]. Interfaces and similar geometric objects defined in pure 2-dimensional critical models are conjectured, and in some cases proven, to satisfy both requirements in the continuum limit. SLE hence describes such diverse systems as percolation κ=6\kappa=6, self-avoiding walks κ=4/3\kappa=4/3, loop-erased random walks κ=2\kappa=2 and level lines of height models κ=4\kappa=4 [2]. It applies to the Ising and 3-states Potts interfaces, both for spin clusters (κ=3\kappa=3 and κ=10/3\kappa=10/3, respectively) and the dual Fortuin Kasteleyn (FK) clusters (κ=16/3\kappa=16/3 and κ=24/5\kappa=24/5), with a duality κ↔κ′=16/κ\kappa\leftrightarrow\kappa^{\prime}=16/\kappa. While these models have been described, prior to SLE, using conformal field theory (CFT), SLE bridges the gap between the algebraic approach of CFT and the geometry of interfaces. The present connections between SLE and CFT [2] focus on boundary-condition changing operators, which generate the curves. They give df=1+κ/8d_{\mathrm{f}}=1+\kappa/8 for the fractal dimension of the interface, i.e. the hull of the SLE trace. Extensions beyond non-minimal CFT [3] are rare.

A tantalizing question is whether CFT methods and SLE help to understand a broader class of scale-invariant 2d complex systems, such as systems with quenched disorder or far from equilibrium. Numerical studies indicate that zero-vorticity lines in 2D-turbulence [4] and domain walls in spin-glasses [5] may be described by SLE. These examples are “far” from any pure CFT, thus the situation may be more favorable for models which are “weak perturbations” of a known CFT. This is e.g. the case for the qq-states Potts model, perturbed by quenched random bond (i.e., temperature) disorder, known to exhibit a stable weak-disorder fixed point for q>2q>2, perturbatively accessible in a q−2q-2 expansion. This has been studied using conformal perturbation theory [6, 7] and transfer-matrix methods [8]. However, geometric properties of interfaces which are crucial for future comparison to SLE were to our knowledge not investigated.

The aim of this Letter is to present results for the fractal dimension of domain walls in the random-temperature Potts model. These are obtained by analytical calculation using conformal perturbation theory inspired by [6, 7], and from two types of large-scale numerics: Monte Carlo simulations using the efficient Wolf-algorithm [10], which allow to keep track of both spin and FK clusters in the same simulation, and transfer-matrix calculations, whose advantage is to make close contact with CFT. The results of all three methods agree nicely.

Let us recall the definition of the model: In terms of the spin variables σi={1,⋯,q}\sigma_{i}=\{1,\cdots,q\} at lattice site ii, the partition function of the qq-states Potts model is

𝒵=∑{σi}eβ​∑⟨i​j⟩Ji​j​δσi​σj∼∑{σi}∏⟨i​j⟩[1−𝗉i​j+𝗉i​j​δσi​σj],{\cal Z}=\sum_{\{\sigma_{i}\}}\mathrm{e}^{\beta\sum_{\left<ij\right>}J_{ij}\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}}\sim\sum_{\{\sigma_{i}\}}\prod_{\left<ij\right>}\left[1-{\sf p}_{ij}+{\sf p}_{ij}\delta_{\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}\right]\ ,

where the sum runs over nearest-neighbor bonds ⟨i,j⟩\left<i,j\right>. The last expression is the spin-cluster expansion, noting 1−𝗉i​j=e−β​Ji​j1-{\sf p}_{ij}=\mathrm{e}^{-\beta J_{ij}}. By expanding in 𝗉i​j{\sf p}_{ij}, it can be rewritten in terms of the Fortuin-Kasteleyn (FK) clusters, composed by placing a bond between neighboring sites with probability 𝗉i​j{\sf p}_{ij}. The pure ferromagnetic model has Ji​j=J>0J_{ij}=J>0, 𝗉i​j=𝗉{\sf p}_{ij}={\sf p}, while in the disordered one the Ji​jJ_{ij} are chosen as i.i.d. random variables. 𝒵∼∑𝒢𝗉|𝒢|​(1−𝗉)|𝒢¯|​q‖𝒢‖,{\cal Z}\sim\sum_{\cal G}{\sf p}^{|{\cal G}|}(1-{\sf p})^{|\overline{\cal G}|}q^{||{\cal G}||}\ ,\quad (1)

Here 𝒢\mathcal{G} runs over all clusters (i.e. domains connected by the above placed bonds), |𝒢|\left|{\cal G}\right| is the number of bonds, |𝒢¯|\left|\overline{\cal G}\right| the not placed bonds, and ‖𝒢‖||{\cal G}|| the number of connected components. The partition sum (1) allows to define the Potts model with non-integer q≥0q\geq 0. For the pure model it has a continuous phase transition for 0≤q≤40\leq q\leq 4, which becomes first order for q>4q>4.

Here we focus on geometrical properties, hence on the operator Φ10​(z)\Phi_{10}(z) which measures [13] the passage of one critical curve at point z→\vec{z}. Indeed, for the pure model, the correlation function ⟨Φ10​(z)​Φ10​(0)⟩0=|z|−4​Δ10\left<\Phi_{10}(z)\Phi_{10}(0)\right>_{0}=|z|^{-4\Delta_{10}} gives the probability that two points lie at the perimeter of the same FK cluster, from which one obtains the fractal dimension of FK domain walls dfFK,pure=2−2​Δ10d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{FK,pure}}=2-2\Delta_{10}, i.e. dfFK=8/5d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{FK}}=8/5 for q=3q=3. Here we compute the corresponding probability for the disordered system. A crucial question is whether Φ10​(z)\Phi_{10}(z) is still the “curve-detecting” operator in the disordered system. This is true at the “critical dimension” p=q=2p=q=2. Increasing pp deforms the operator adiabatically. Since the latter is a physical observable, it is an eigenoperator of the RG. We must check if there is an operator at p=2p=2 which (i) has the same dimension as Φ1,0\Phi_{1,0}, and (ii) appears in the sub-algebra generated by Φ1,0\Phi_{1,0} and Φ1,2\Phi_{1,2}. If such an operator exists, it mixes with Φ1,0\Phi_{1,0}, and the curve-detecting operator will be one of the eigenoperators of the RG flow involving Φ10\Phi_{10}. We checked the absence of such an operator: thus, at least for small p−2p-2, Φ10\Phi_{10} is the curve-detecting operator.

The structure of the result and the logarithmic divergence remain valid for larger values of pp, with the parameters replaced by rational functions of pp. This behavior is consistent with the appearance of operators of canonical dimensions 11 and 00 (different from the identity) in the OPE of ε\varepsilon with Φ1,0\Phi_{1,0} as discussed in a similar case in [17]. Even more surprisingly, we attempted to perform the same calculation for the fractal dimension of spin interfaces, using the operator Φ01\Phi_{01} as curve detector. There the equivalent of (7) does not exist: At least we were not able to construct a 4-point function, which satisfies the differential equation induced by the 0-vector condition associated to ε=Φ12\varepsilon=\Phi_{12} at level 2, which is unique-valued, and reproduces the correct OPE in the limit of u→1u\to 1.

We now discuss our numerical results. For the Monte Carlo simulations we use the Wolff cluster algorithm [10]. It consists in randomly choosing a spin, and then joining with probability 𝗉{\sf p} nearest-neighbor spins to belong to the same cluster. This procedure is repeated until no nearest neighbor can be joined anymore. 𝗉{\sf p} itself is a quenched random variable on the edges of the lattice, taken from the symmetric bimodal distribution {𝗉1,𝗉2}={1−exp⁡(−βc​J1),1−exp⁡(−βc​J2)}\left\{{\sf p}_{1},{\sf p}_{2}\right\}=\left\{1-\exp(-\beta_{c}J_{1}),1-\exp(-\beta_{c}J_{2})\right\}. The choice 𝗉1​𝗉2=q{\sf p}_{1}{\sf p}_{2}=q ensures that the system is at its critical point [14]. We use J1=J2J_{1}=J_{2} for the pure, and J1/J2=10J_{1}/J_{2}=10 for the random-bond disordered system. Once the cluster is constructed, we assign to it with equal probability one of the qq colors, as long as this is consistent with the boundary conditions (BC) discussed below. Wolff has shown [10] that this algorithm produces the correct statistical weight of the Potts model, is ergodic, and that the critical slowing down is reduced compared to ordinary Monte Carlo algorithms. In addition, it allows to track both spin and FK clusters. In the simulations, we imposed boundary conditions which create a domain wall which span the lattice as was already done by Gamsa and Cardy [15]. We considered various types of conformally invariant boundary conditions: “fluctuating” (a/a¯a/\bar{a}), “fixed” (a/ba/b), and “free” (a/freea/\text{free}), all of them giving the same result in the large-size limit.

We measured the fractal dimension from the average length ll of the domain wall as a function of the linear size LL of the lattice ⟨l⟩¯≃Ldf\overline{\langle l\rangle}\simeq L^{d_{\mathrm{f}}}, where ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle denotes the thermal average and ⋯¯\overline{\cdots} the disorder average [25]. The results presented here are obtained with a thermal average over ≃106×τ\simeq 10^{6}\times\tau for the pure system and a disorder average over ≃105\simeq 10^{5} configurations for the disordered system. τ\tau is the autocorrelation time which was first determined for each size, see [16] for details. Our simulations show that for the pure system, all these domain walls have asymptotically the same fractal dimension, with the exception of the common domain wall for fixed BC, which has dimension one. In Fig. 1 we plot the effective fractal dimension versus LL. As L→∞L\to\infty the fractal dimensions of the pure system converge to the values predicted by conformal field theory, dfspin=1712d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{spin}}=\frac{17}{12}, and dfFK=85d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{FK}}=\frac{8}{5}, corroborating partial results by Gamsa and Cardy [15]. Our estimate from all BC, extrapolated to an infinite system gives dfspin=1.416±0.002d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{spin}}=1.416\pm 0.002, and dfFK=1.599±0.002d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{FK}}=1.599\pm 0.002. For the disordered system we find

dfspin=1.401±0.003,dfFK=1.614±0.003d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{spin}}=1.401\pm 0.003\ ,\qquad d_{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{FK}}=1.614\pm 0.003 (10)

This is in excellent agreement with our analytical result (6). We have also checked the SLE duality relation κ​κ′=16\kappa\kappa^{\prime}=16. Using dκ=1+κ8d_{\mathrm{\kappa}}=1+\frac{\kappa}{8}, we find for the pure system κspin=3.328±0.016\kappa^{\mathrm{spin}}=3.328\pm 0.016, κFK=4.792±0.016\kappa^{\mathrm{FK}}=4.792\pm 0.016, and κspin​κFK=15.95±0.13\kappa^{\mathrm{spin}}\kappa^{\mathrm{FK}}=15.95\pm 0.13. For the disordered system, we find κspin=3.208±0.024\kappa^{\mathrm{spin}}=3.208\pm 0.024, κFK=4.912±0.024\kappa^{\mathrm{FK}}=4.912\pm 0.024, and κspin​κFK=15.76±0.20\kappa^{\mathrm{spin}}\kappa^{\mathrm{FK}}=15.76\pm 0.20.

In the transfer-matrix approach, we studied the FK clusters in the equivalent loop formulation [19]. The loops are defined on the medial lattice as the external and internal hulls of the FK clusters. The random bonds were again drawn from a bimodal distribution, with an equal number of strong and weak bonds [21]. The strength of the disorder is conveniently characterized by the parameter ss [20] defined by J1/J2=ln⁡(1+s​q)/ln⁡(1+q/s)J_{1}/J_{2}=\ln(1+s\sqrt{q})/\ln(1+\sqrt{q}/s), with q=3q=3. For a given fixed realization of the random bonds on long cylinders of length M=105M=10^{5} and circumference L=4,6,…,12L=4,6,\ldots,12 lattice spacings (for the medial lattice) the corresponding free energy fj​(L)f_{j}(L), normalized per lattice site, was computed from the leading Lyapunov exponent of the corresponding product of random transfer matrices. The transfer direction was taken axial with respect to the medial lattice (hence diagonal with respect to the original square lattice supporting the Potts spins) [19]. Three different topological sectors were considered, corresponding to enforcing j=0,2,4j=0,2,4 loop segments to propagate along the length direction of the cylinder. The fluctuations of these free energies were studied by averaging over at least M′=105M^{\prime}=10^{5} independent cylinders.

Conformal field theory predicts [22] that f0​(L)¯=f0​(∞)¯−π​c6​L2+AL4+⋯\overline{f_{0}(L)}=\overline{f_{0}(\infty)}-\frac{\pi c}{6L^{2}}+\frac{A}{L^{4}}+\cdots, where cc is the effective central charge and AA a non-universal constant. Applying this to three consecutive LL gives estimates c⁡(L−4,L−2,L)c(L-4,L-2,L) shown in the left panel of Fig. 2. The fixed-point value s∗s^{*} of the disorder strength corresponds to the locus of the maximum of cc, and is estimated as s∗=4.0±0.3s^{*}=4.0\pm 0.3 (using also data not shown here), improving on the value s∗=3.5±0.5s^{*}=3.5\pm 0.5 reported earlier [20]. The effective central charge of the disordered model is estimated as c⁡(s∗)=0.8024±0.0003c(s^{*})=0.8024\pm 0.0003, in excellent agreement with the three-loop perturbative result [7] c≃0.8025c\simeq 0.8025.

Correlation functions Gj​(M)G_{j}(M) are defined as the probability of having jj loop segments propagate over a distance MM along the cylinder axis without joining up. They are related to the free energy gaps through Δ​fj​(L)≡fj​(L)−f0​(L)=−1M​L​ln⁡Gj​(M)\Delta f_{j}(L)\equiv f_{j}(L)-f_{0}(L)=\frac{-1}{ML}\ln G_{j}(M). Their disorder-averaged nn’th moment can be extracted from the cumulant expansion [8] ln⁡(Gj)n¯=n​ln⁡Gj¯+12​n2​(ln⁡Gj−ln⁡Gj¯)2¯+⋯\ln\overline{(G_{j})^{n}}=n\overline{\ln G_{j}}+\frac{1}{2}n^{2}\overline{(\ln G_{j}-\overline{\ln G_{j}})^{2}}+\cdots, where the quantities on the r.h.s. are self-averaging. Only the first two cumulants contribute significantly. CFT predicts [23] that −1M​L​ln⁡(Gj)n¯=2​π​xjL2+BL4+⋯\frac{-1}{ML}\ln\overline{(G_{j})^{n}}=\frac{2\pi x_{j}}{L^{2}}+\frac{B}{L^{4}}+\cdots, where the nn-dependent conformal weights xjx_{j} are related to the desired (multi)fractal dimensions via dj=2−xjd_{j}=2-x_{j}. For n=1n=1, we have d2=dfFKd_{2}=d_{\rm f}^{\rm FK} defined above; d4d_{4} gives the dimension of “red bonds” (whose removal disconnects a cluster). As seen from the right panel of Fig. 2, the effective values of djd_{j} depend strongly on ss, so accuracy for s∗s^{*} is important [20]. Using s∗=4.0±0.3s^{*}=4.0\pm 0.3 we estimate d2=1.615±0.002d_{2}=1.615\pm 0.002, in excellent agreement with (6) and (10).

To conclude, our analytical and numerical results for the fractal dimension of FK domain walls agree well. Fractal dimensions of spin interfaces have been determined from numerics and seem in agreement with the duality relation suggested by SLE. Pending questions under investigation are possible multiscaling, the fractal dimensions of spin interfaces and SLE type observables.
